hook.en: Gandhi agreed to a refund of only twenty-five per cent when he could have pressed for more. Why would a careful negotiator do that?

objectives.en: Explain the settlement and why Gandhi accepted it
Describe the social and cultural work in Champaran
Identify the lessons of self-reliance and freedom from fear

narration.en: Gandhi agreed to a refund of only twenty-five per cent when he could have pressed for more. Why would a careful negotiator do that?

body.en: An official commission of inquiry was set up, with Gandhi as the sole representative of the peasants. The planters agreed to refund money to the peasants, and Gandhi accepted twenty-five per cent. He explained that the amount mattered less than the fact that the planters had been obliged to surrender part of the money and their prestige. Within a few years the British planters gave up their estates, which went back to the peasants, and indigo sharecropping disappeared.

points.en: Commission of inquiry; Gandhi represents the peasants
Refund of twenty-five per cent accepted
The planters lost money and prestige
Within a few years the planters left; land returned to peasants

say.en: At the centre is the Champaran movement of 1917.
It was the first triumph of civil disobedience in India.
The peasants learnt to stand up without fear.
Gandhi refused Andrews's help to teach self-reliance.
Breaking the planters' prestige mattered more than money.
Schools, hygiene and health work changed daily life.
It showed a leader working with and for the poor.

body.en: Gandhi did not stop at the legal victory. With volunteers, he opened primary schools in six villages; Kasturba taught cleanliness, and a doctor volunteered to treat the sick. Gandhi refused C. F. Andrews's offer to stay and help, because depending on an Englishman would show weakness: the peasants had to learn to rely on themselves. The real lesson was freedom from fear.

problem.en: Why did Gandhi agree to a settlement of only twenty-five per cent?

steps.en: State the amount: twenty-five per cent refund.
Give his reason: the money mattered less than the principle.

answer.en: Gandhi felt the amount was less important than the fact that the planters were forced to return part of the money and their prestige. The peasants learnt they had rights, and within a few years the planters left.
